_schema_note: Each chunk: id (unique), title, region_tags (lowercase keywords used for retrieval scoring against the explanation's node names/regions), and text (the planner-facing knowledge). Regions in region_tags MUST match the labels emitted by models/explainer/node_names.py so retrieval lines up with the explanation. Keep text factual and sourced from public LADOT/Caltrans corridor information — no invented capacities.

chunks.title: I-10 Santa Monica Freeway corridor
chunks.text: I-10 (Santa Monica Fwy) is the primary east-west corridor linking Downtown LA to the Westside and Santa Monica. Recurrent PM bottleneck at the I-10/I-110 interchange downtown and the La Cienega/Robertson stretch. Caltrans ramp meters operate on most eastbound on-ramps during peak. Parallel relief arterials: Olympic Blvd and Pico Blvd (both signal-coordinated by LADOT ATSAC).

chunks.title: I-110 Harbor Freeway corridor
chunks.text: I-110 (Harbor Fwy) runs north-south through Downtown LA toward South LA and the ports. Chronic congestion at the 4-level interchange (I-110/US-101) and the I-10 merge. Has HOV/ExpressLanes (Metro ExpressLanes) between Adams Blvd and the 105 that can be opened to general purpose during incidents. Figueroa St and Vermont Ave are the parallel north-south arterials.

chunks.title: US-101 Hollywood Freeway corridor
chunks.text: US-101 (Hollywood Fwy) connects Downtown LA through Hollywood toward the San Fernando Valley over the Cahuenga Pass. Bottleneck at the US-101/I-110 four-level and at the Cahuenga Pass grade. Surface relief: Sunset Blvd and Santa Monica Blvd, both ATSAC signal-coordinated.

chunks.title: I-405 San Diego Freeway corridor
chunks.text: I-405 (San Diego Fwy) is the north-south Westside spine over the Sepulveda Pass connecting the San Fernando Valley to West LA, LAX and the South Bay. One of the most congested segments in the US; Sepulveda Pass saturates in both peaks. Sepulveda Blvd is the parallel arterial. Ramp metering is active pass-wide.

chunks.title: Glendale/Burbank freeways (SR-134, I-5, SR-2)
chunks.text: SR-134 (Ventura Fwy) and I-5 (Golden State Fwy) carry Glendale/Burbank traffic between the eastern San Fernando Valley and Pasadena/Downtown. Key merge congestion at the I-5/SR-134/SR-2 interchange. Brand Blvd, San Fernando Rd and Colorado Blvd are the surface reliefs. Metro is limited here, so demand is car-dominant.

chunks.title: San Fernando Valley freeways (US-101, I-405, SR-118)
chunks.text: The San Fernando Valley feeds US-101 (Ventura Fwy, east-west) and I-405 (over the Sepulveda Pass, south). Ventura Blvd is the primary east-west surface arterial and Sepulveda/Van Nuys Blvd the primary north-south. Congestion builds westbound US-101 in the AM peak and southbound I-405 approaching the pass.

chunks.title: Known recurrent bottlenecks (LA basin)
chunks.text: Recurrent bottlenecks a planner should assume unless told otherwise: (1) I-10/I-110 downtown interchange, PM peak; (2) I-405 Sepulveda Pass, both peaks; (3) US-101/I-110 four-level, AM peak; (4) I-5/SR-134 interchange, PM peak. These are structural (geometry/merges), so upstream metering and reroute-before-the-merge are the levers, not signal timing at the interchange itself.

chunks.title: Signal-timing control (LADOT ATSAC) constraints
chunks.text: LADOT's ATSAC/ATCS system adaptively controls ~4,900 signalized intersections and can push a special timing plan to a corridor within minutes from the Transportation Management Center. Practical constraints: coordinated corridors (Olympic, Pico, Wilshire, Sunset, Figueroa, Vermont) can have green-band extended by 10-20% for up to ~30 min before side-street queues become unacceptable; changes need TMC operator action, not field crews.

chunks.title: Transit alternatives (Metro rail/bus)
chunks.text: Metro rail relief options by area: B/D (Red/Purple) Lines under Wilshire and through Hollywood; A Line (Blue/Gold) Downtown to Long Beach and to Pasadena; E Line (Expo) Downtown to Santa Monica along the I-10; ExpressLanes bus on I-110. Transit is a viable diversion lever only where a parallel rail line exists (Wilshire, Expo/I-10, Harbor/I-110, Pasadena A Line); the Valley and Glendale/Burbank are largely rail-poor.

chunks.title: Incident-history summary
chunks.text: Historically, non-recurrent delay in this network is dominated by incidents on I-10, I-110 and I-405 during peaks; a single blocking incident on the Sepulveda Pass or the downtown interchanges can add 15-25 min of network delay within 30 min. Fast detection + upstream diversion is the highest-value response. Caltrans/CHP clearance times average 20-40 min for injury incidents.

chunks.title: Approximate road capacities (per direction)
chunks.text: Planning capacities (per lane, per direction): urban freeway lane ~1,900-2,200 veh/hr at free flow, dropping to ~1,500 in stop-and-go; major coordinated arterial lane ~700-900 veh/hr including signal delay. A freeway loses ~40-50% of throughput once it breaks down, which is why keeping flow above the critical density (metering, diversion BEFORE the queue) matters more than reacting after.
